title: Going the Distance With a Cursed Wish
subtitle: This week: Coyote vs. Acme's boulder, Nolan's Odyssey, The Dog Stars, and the wish in Obsession you can't take back once you've thrown the first jab
excerpt: A week of bag work and roadwork filtered through a Wile E. Coyote legal drama, a Homeric slog across the wine-dark sea, a post-collapse survival story, and a cursed-wish horror film that plays like a fight you're not allowed to stop. The through-line is the same one every session on the bag teaches you: once it's started, quitting isn't actually on the table.
intro_md:
Wrapped my hands this morning in that grey stretch before the gym properly wakes up, the heater ticking, nobody else in yet. There's a specific kind of quiet in an empty gym that I don't get anywhere else, not even on a dawn run when the streets are still mine. Both have the same rule though: you showed up, so now you finish it.

That rule is basically the spine of everything I watched this week. A coyote who cannot stop pushing his boulder up the hill. A man rowing home for ten years because the alternative is not rowing home at all. A father in a dying world who keeps flying his plane because stopping means giving up on the last thing worth flying toward. And a horror film about a wish you cannot unwish once you've made it, which is the closest thing I've seen on screen to what a scheduled six-rounder actually feels like once the bell goes.

film_blurbs.title: Coyote vs. Acme (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
I did not expect the best Albuquerque-set legal drama I've seen in years to also be a Wile E. Coyote movie, but here we are. The premise is a class-action suit against the ACME corporation for decades of faulty products, and it plays it entirely straight, which is what makes it so funny.

Underneath the joke there's something that landed harder than I expected. Coyote never actually catches the Roadrunner and never really wants to, not deep down. He just wants the process. That's most of my week on the bag, honestly. Nobody's handing out a trophy for a good session of mitt work. You just show up and push the boulder again tomorrow, and if you're doing it right you sort of like the boulder.

There's a genuine warmth in how the film treats its central duo, coyote and rock, more or less as friends stuck in the same Sisyphean bit. I laughed more than I expected and got weirdly choked up near the end, which is not a sentence I thought I'd write about a movie with an anvil gag in it.

film_blurbs.title: The Odyssey (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
Ten years to get home. That's the whole pitch, and it's also more or less the shape of a long training camp if you stretch the metaphor far enough, which I am always willing to do. Homer's poem is fundamentally about endurance dressed up as adventure, a man absorbing punishment from gods, monsters, and his own bad decisions, and refusing to stop moving toward one fixed point.

What struck me watching it is how much of the story is just about the body giving out and the will not agreeing to that. Odysseus gets shipwrecked, starved, seduced, delayed, and every time the film resets him to zero and makes him start again. That's roadwork. That's rounds four through eight of sparring when your legs have gone and your corner is telling you it's still winnable if you just keep your hands up.

It's a big, long, demanding watch, and I mean that as a compliment. Some films you enjoy. This one you go the distance with.

film_blurbs.title: The Dog Stars (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
Adapted from Peter Heller's novel, this is a quiet, bruised film about a man flying a small plane over a depopulated world, keeping a routine going because the routine is the only thing standing between him and giving up entirely. There's a rhythm to his day, fuel checks, patrol laps, small rituals, that reminded me a lot of the boring mechanical parts of a fight camp nobody puts in the trailer. The wraps, the same six warm-up drills, the walk to the gym in weather you'd rather not walk in.

The film is more interested in endurance as a psychological act than a physical one, which fits. Most of what gets you through mile ten of a long run, or the last thirty seconds of a round you're losing, isn't strength. It's just refusing to let the day's structure collapse.

film_blurbs.title: The Whisper Man (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
This one sits closer to crime thriller than horror, but it's got a creeping, patient dread running under the surface that I found harder to shake than plenty of films that lean harder into scares. A father relocates with his son after a loss, into a town with its own history of missing children, and the film takes its time letting that history seep back in.

It's a slow-burn watch, more about dread accumulating than jump scares landing, and I mean that as a compliment given how much of the genre right now goes the opposite way. Worth putting on if you want something that unsettles you at the pace of a long jog rather than a sprint.

horror_deepdive.title: The Wish You Can't Take Back
horror_deepdive.body_md:
Curry Barker's [feature directorial debut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obsession_(2025_film)) is a cursed-wish horror film, which is one of the oldest engines in the genre. Somebody wants something badly enough to make a bargain for it, and the bargain turns out to have teeth. What makes Barker's version land is how contemporary the mechanism feels. This isn't a monkey's paw or a witch in the woods. [Obsession gives chilling modern relevance to a classic tale of a wish gone wrong](https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/reviews/obsession-curry-barker-plays-twisted-ideas-manosphere-violent-make-wish-horror), and the wish itself comes wrapped in the language of an app or a subscription service.

The detail that stuck with me is the customer service call. At some point [Bear calls One Wish Willow customer service and learns the wish only ends if he or Nikki dies](https://movies.fandom.com/wiki/Obsession_(2025)). Read that back. There is a support line. There is presumably a hold queue. And the answer, when it finally comes, is that the only two exits from this thing are somebody's death. Not a refund, not a safe word, not a form you fill out to cancel. [Bear wants this to end, but he can't take his wish back](https://nofilmschool.com/obsession-ending-explained), and that single fact turns the second half of the film into a countdown with exactly one door out.

I kept thinking about that phone call in relation to the mental furniture of a fight. Before you sign on for a bout, or even before you commit to a hard sparring session, there's a version of you weighing it up, deciding whether this is worth doing. That version of you has options. He can pull out, take a lighter camp, tell the coach he's not ready. But once the gloves are laced and you've touched them at centre ring, that guy is gone. There's no line you can call. The fight doesn't have a customer service department. You made the wish the day you agreed to it, and now the only two ways out are the final bell or somebody not getting up.

This is, I think, the actual psychological weight of going the distance, and why the phrase gets used so casually when the reality of it is fairly brutal. Distance isn't a number of rounds. It's the acceptance, made in advance, that quitting is not an option you get to reach for once things start going badly. You don't get to renegotiate in round seven because round seven turned out to be worse than you'd planned for. The contract was signed in round one, or really it was signed the day you agreed to the fight at all.

Roadwork teaches a smaller version of the same lesson. Ten miles out from the house at dawn means ten miles back, regardless of what your legs feel like at mile six. Nobody's coming to get you. There's no wish you can unmake halfway through a training run just because the hill turned out to be steeper than the map suggested. You made the deal when you laced up and shut the front door behind you.

What Obsession understands, and what makes it more unsettling than a straightforward monster movie, is that the horror isn't a thing chasing you. It's a rule you agreed to when you weren't thinking clearly about what agreeing meant. Every fighter who's ever taken a beating in a fight they should have thrown in the towel on, except there was no towel, knows exactly what that rule feels like from the inside.

closing_md: Hands are taped, the bag's still swinging slightly from this morning, and there's a run pencilled in for tomorrow that I am already negotiating with myself about. No customer service line for that either. See you next week.

For Coyote vs. Acme I leaned on the boulder-pushing/bag-work comparison. Do you have an actual repetitive drill this week (mitts, a specific bag combo, roadwork loop) that captures that same 'you kind of like the grind' feeling better than my guess?

The Odyssey blurb uses a generic 'rounds four through eight when your legs go' image. Do you have a real sparring or fight memory of hitting that wall, or a specific long run where you had to talk yourself through the second half?

The Obsession deep-dive leans hard on the 'no towel to throw in' framing. Have you ever actually been in a session, spar or fight, where stopping genuinely wasn't an option and you had to just absorb it? That would anchor the whole section better than my hypothetical.
